headline: High risk of prompt-injection, data leakage, and destructive command execution when Firecrawl feeds Open Interpreter by default.

A_prompt_injection.rationale: Firecrawl ingests raw web content and exposes MCP-compatible/API outputs; Open Interpreter reads clipboard/files/stdin and can execute instructions from content it processes. That creates a direct instruction-injection path if Firecrawl output is copied or piped into Open Interpreter. Both profiles document the bridge surfaces, so this is more than speculative.
conditions: IF Firecrawl output is copied into Open Interpreter clipboard or stdin, injected instructions can be executed.
IF Open Interpreter is run with --auto_run, malicious web text from Firecrawl can trigger actions without confirmation.
mitigations: Disable auto-run in Open Interpreter.
Paste only sanitized excerpts, not raw Firecrawl output.
Use a provenance tag or delimiter wrapper for all Firecrawl text.
Run Open Interpreter in a separate OS account or container.
requires-engineering: add content filtering between Firecrawl and Open Interpreter.

B_data_leakage.rationale: Firecrawl handles API keys and broad network egress; Open Interpreter can read the entire local filesystem and has broad egress too. If Firecrawl outputs are stored in shared files or copied into Open Interpreter, secrets from either side can be exposed or exfiltrated. The pair’s documented surfaces make leakage plausible in default desktop workflows.
conditions: IF Firecrawl artifacts are written to a shared local file, Open Interpreter can read them.
IF Open Interpreter is given access to files containing FIRECRAWL_API_KEY or other secrets, those secrets can be transmitted over network egress.
mitigations: Store Firecrawl outputs in a dedicated directory with restrictive permissions.
Remove secrets from any file passed to Open Interpreter.
Use separate OS users for the two agents.
Rotate exposed API keys after any shared-file workflow.
requires-engineering: enforce secret redaction before handoff.

C_capability_conflict.rationale: Open Interpreter can write the filesystem, modify git state, and spawn subprocesses; Firecrawl supports multiple instances and broad API/network activity. If both operate on the same workspace, concurrent writes or git mutations can overwrite each other or corrupt state. The profiles explicitly show overlapping mutable surfaces, so conflict risk is substantial.
conditions: IF both agents target the same directory, file overwrites or partial writes can occur.
IF Open Interpreter commits while Firecrawl-generated files are being updated, git state can become inconsistent.
mitigations: Assign each agent a separate working directory.
Serialize writes with a lock file.
Avoid letting Open Interpreter modify git state in the Firecrawl workspace.
Use read-only mounts for Firecrawl outputs.
requires-engineering: add orchestrator-level locking.

D_cascading_error.rationale: Firecrawl produces scraped web content and structured data; Open Interpreter can act on that output with shell, package install, and filesystem privileges. If Open Interpreter treats Firecrawl results as authoritative, a bad scrape or injected page content can cascade into destructive local actions. The downstream authority is documented in Open Interpreter, while Firecrawl supplies the upstream content.
conditions: IF Open Interpreter uses Firecrawl output as direct input to shell commands, errors can propagate into destructive actions.
IF Firecrawl returns malformed or adversarial content and Open Interpreter does not verify it, the cascade can affect files or packages.
mitigations: Require human review before any shell command derived from Firecrawl output.
Validate Firecrawl output against a schema before use.
Disable package installation for automated handoffs.
Log and diff all generated commands before execution.
requires-engineering: add verification gates between agents.

E_compliance.rationale: Firecrawl touches web content and API keys, while Open Interpreter can access the entire local machine and uses model-provider APIs. If regulated or sensitive data is scraped into local files, the pair can create retention and residency mismatches, especially because Open Interpreter’s default self-isolation is none. The profiles do not prove a specific jurisdiction breach, so medium is the highest supportable level.
conditions: IF regulated data is scraped by Firecrawl and then stored locally, Open Interpreter may retain it on the host filesystem.
IF model-provider APIs are configured for Open Interpreter, local data may leave the machine under provider-specific retention terms.
mitigations: Avoid scraping regulated data into local files.
Use a dedicated retention policy for Firecrawl outputs.
Run Open Interpreter in a disposable workspace.
Review provider retention settings before use.
requires-engineering: document residency and retention controls.
